title: On Making $SE(2)$-Invariant Networks Optimal
claim: A full architecture is built hierarchically from simple stacked blocks, whose key layer turns local features into invariants through a small set of operations.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, zoom-in from network to block to layer
description: Three panels show the architecture at decreasing scale. (a) is a vertical stack of gray rounded boxes: Stem, Stage 1 to 3 (each N_i × Blocks), then green GAP and MLP boxes, joined by arrows. (b) zooms into one block inside a gray rounded container. A blue trapezoid labeled Mom/Inv Layer feeds a green Conv 1x1, Norm, a dashed Down Scale box and a plus node, then Act. A residual skip arrow runs along the right side. (c) is a light-blue trapezoid titled Projection into Moments. It shows colored boxes Type 0 to Type n, shaded from teal to purple. Arrows and ⊗ nodes combine them into teal output boxes labeled Construction of Invariants. Panel captions sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the colorful panel (c).
caption: Overview of the proposed invariant convolutional architecture. (a) The overall network architecture obtained by stacking the proposed blocks. (b) The invariant convolution block, combining a moment layer and an invariant layer within a residual structure. (c) Illustration of the invariant layer, showing how moment responses are combined to produce rotation-invariant features.
abstract: Respecting a-priori known symmetries of underlying data is a key principle in designing efficient neural architectures. Convolutional neural networks are a canonical example, encoding translation equivariance. Extending this inductive bias to richer symmetry groups such as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ in the most effective way possible is an ongoing architectural and computational challenge. Building on classical invariant theory, we derive invariant feature maps that are provably optimal: minimal and information-preserving with respect to the symmetry group. Our construction is designed to integrate seamlessly into standard architectures, requiring no modification to nonlinearities or normalization layers. As a concrete implementation, we introduce a plug-and-play module for convolutional neural networks that enforces $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ invariance, capturing both translations and rotations within standard architectures. The resulting models are both efficient and expressive. Experiments show competitive or improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art equivariant methods at significantly lower computational cost. Finally, we provide a theoretical and empirical analysis of the relationship between equivariance and invariance, offering insight into their roles in controlling robustness and flexibility.
